title: Load Shedding

validation.research: Six primary references: AWS establishes Load Shedding, early refusal, goodput, rejection cost and overload testing; Google SRE explains variable request cost, resource utilization, criticality, degraded responses and client-side throttling; Envoy distinguishes resource-pressure overload actions from upstream circuit breaking; RFC 9110 defines 503 temporary overload and optional Retry-After; RFC 6585 defines 429 rate refusal; Python documents the actual lock, event and owned-thread operations. Admission control is a mechanism and overload protection a broader goal, not exact aliases. Load balancing spreads requests while shedding refuses some; degraded responses are a separate way to reduce work. The ticket scenario, weighted policy, event-gated code and native figures are original teaching material.

runnable_example.verification: Actual article fences run unchanged on Python 3.11+. Four-line output verifies held cost two, cost-two refusal, cost-one success and later reuse. Strict integer validation rejects Boolean/fractional/negative/zero inputs, and over-capacity cost is ValueError even at saturation; no invalid/refused callback runs or budget is claimed. Exact equality is admitted. Falsy results and ValueError/TimeoutError/cancellation-like BaseException preserve identity and return exactly the claimed cost; non-callable action failure also returns cost. Nested callback calls prove execution is outside the accounting lock. Ten simultaneous cost-two actions against five units admit exactly two held callbacks and refuse eight, leaving one unit for a light action at equality; execution occurs on caller threads. Refusal never adds waiters or changes occupied cost. Independent instances do not share budget. A real callback-owned TemporaryFile remains open through gated finally cleanup and budget remains occupied even when an observer stops waiting; closure precedes result observation and capacity reuse. All owned threads are released/joined and thread inventory returns to baseline. No hardware, rate, fairness, priority, deadline, cancellation, fleet quota, HTTP response or measured production goodput guarantee is inferred.

example_limits: New canonical article using established Load Shedding title. Admission control is the possible mechanism and overload protection the broader goal, not exact aliases. Original ticket-service example uses a retained process-local LoadShedder with positive integer capacity and server-assigned integer request costs. A Lock atomically claims only fitting cost; callbacks execute on caller threads outside the lock and finally return exactly the claimed cost after local action/cleanup. Capacity three with one held cost-two action refuses a second cost-two operation without invocation, permits a cost-one action at equality, and later admits heavy work after owned release/join. Invalid or over-capacity costs are ValueError policy errors rather than transient Overloaded refusals. The event-gated experiment supplies no waiting queue, execution pool, hardware reservation, rate limiter, priority/fairness guarantee, fleet-wide accounting, deadline, cancellation, HTTP response, durable acceptance or remote rollback. Estimated cost is not measured CPU/memory, and callback work/cleanup must finish before return. Optional-recommendation criticality is a separate policy context; the fit rule does not implement it. Tests verify invalid policy versus temporary occupancy, cost equality, nested callback execution outside the lock, exact result/error propagation, ten real competing weighted actions, no invocation/claim on refusal, actual file cleanup before budget release, stopped observer waiting, independent instances, full reuse and owned thread joining. The work costs are trusted estimates; no hardware or actual production-goodput benchmark is inferred.
